name: Southern Ming and the Kingdom of Tungning
summary: Ming loyalist courts that fought on in southern China after the Qing took Beijing (1644); Koxinga’s family carried on from Taiwan as the Kingdom of Tungning until the Qing conquered it in 1683.

knownFor.label: Queue order
knownFor.note: Qing order to shave the head, resisted by Ming loyalists.

location.value: Southern China from Nanjing to Guangdong, Guangxi and Yunnan, plus the Fujian coast around Xiamen and, from 1662, Taiwan.

terrain.value: The lower Yangtze plain, the hills and mountains of the south and southwest, the Fujian coast and islands such as Xiamen and Jinmen, and western Taiwan’s plains.

climate.value: Humid subtropical in south China and Taiwan, with hot, rainy summers, monsoon winds and typhoons along the coast.

resources.value: Rice lands of the south, silk and porcelain for export, sugar and deerskins from Taiwan, and the sea trade run by the Zheng family.

population.value: Tens of millions in the regions they briefly held.

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages and farming land around a royal capital.

disease.value: Epidemics followed war and famine; many Zheng soldiers and settlers died of disease in Taiwan’s first years after 1661.

migration.value: Tens of thousands of soldiers and settlers from Fujian moved to Taiwan after 1661, while the Qing coastal evacuation (from 1661) uprooted many coastal people.

economicBase.value: Rice and sugar farming, land taxes, and above all the Zheng family’s overseas trade in silk, sugar and deerskins with Japan and Southeast Asia.

tradeRoutes.value: Maritime trade with Japan and Southeast Asia (Zheng family).

wealth.value: The Zheng trading network, built by Zheng Zhilong, was one of the richest in East Asia and paid for Koxinga’s armies and fleets.

moneyAndTax.value: Ming-style copper coins such as the Yongli tongbao, land and grain taxes, and fees on trade, including passes sold to merchant ships.

inequality.value: Rulers and nobles above farmers; some slavery or bonded labour.

governmentType.value: Rival Ming princes as emperors; Zheng family rule in Taiwan.

keyRulers.value: Hongguang Emperor. Yongli Emperor. Koxinga (Zheng Chenggong).

succession.value: Disputed among Ming princes: the Hongguang (1644–45), Longwu (1645–46) and Yongli (1646–62) emperors; in Taiwan the Zheng ruled father to son.

institutions.value: Ming-style courts with ministries and officials; in Taiwan Chen Yonghua set up schools, examinations and the Confucius Temple.

stability.value: Very unstable: each court lasted only a few years, and the Yongli Emperor was driven from Guangdong into Guangxi, Yunnan and finally Burma.

eliteConflict.value: Rival courts and generals: the Shaowu and Yongli courts fought each other in 1646, and the general Sun Kewang turned on the Yongli court.

armyAndTech.value: Ming loyalist armies, former rebel forces under Li Dingguo, and Koxinga’s large war fleets with cannon and armoured “iron men” infantry.

majorWars.value: Qing conquest of the south; siege of Fort Zeelandia (1661–62).

territoryChange.value: Steadily lost the south to the Qing: Nanjing in 1645, Fujian in 1646 and Yunnan in 1659; Taiwan was won from the Dutch in 1662 and lost in 1683.

alliancesRivals.value: Fought the Qing throughout; Koxinga drove the Dutch East India Company out of Taiwan (1662), and Tungning later traded with Japan and the English.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; the period is better known for loyalist writers and naval warfare.

scienceEducation.value: Confucian scholars served the courts; thinkers such as Wang Fuzhi and Huang Zongxi supported the loyalists, and Taiwan gained its first Confucian schools.

openness.value: Open to sea trade with Japan, Southeast Asia and Europeans; the Zheng depended on commerce, which the Qing tried to cut off.

communicationTransport.value: Rivers, coastal shipping and footpaths; Zheng junks linked Xiamen and Taiwan with Nagasaki and Southeast Asian ports.

languageWriting.value: Chinese, written in Chinese characters; people spoke southern Chinese languages such as Hokkien and Cantonese.

artsArchitecture.value: The Confucius Temple in Tainan, built in 1665 under the Zheng family’s Tungning kingdom as Taiwan’s first Confucian temple and school.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the Ming dynasty and Han Chinese customs, shown by refusing the Qing order (1645) to shave the head and wear the queue.

dailyLife.value: Village farming households growing rice and sugar, disrupted by war, heavy taxes and the Qing coastal evacuation.

neighbours.value: The Qing dynasty to the north, Dutch Formosa until 1662, Tokugawa Japan, Spanish Manila, and Burma, where the Yongli Emperor fled.

ideasReligions.value: Ming loyalism and Confucian ideas of duty to the rightful dynasty, along with worship of Mazu, the sea goddess, among Fujian sailors.

colonisation.value: Koxinga besieged Fort Zeelandia and ended Dutch rule in Taiwan in February 1662; Tungning then settled Han farmers on the island.

riseSignals.value: The fall of Beijing to Li Zicheng’s rebels and then the Qing (1644) led Ming officials to enthrone the Hongguang Emperor at Nanjing.

peakPeriod.value: Koxinga’s Yangtze campaign (1659) reached the walls of Nanjing before it was defeated; Li Dingguo also won victories in the southwest in 1652.

declineSignals.value: The Yongli Emperor was handed over by Burma and killed in Kunming (1662); Koxinga died the same year, and Tungning surrendered in 1683.

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles and foreign reports; figures are estimates.
